awd_titl_txt: Collaborative Research: RAPID: Hurricane impacts on hydrogeology and nutrient geochemistry in karstic coastline
awd_abstract_narration:
Hurricane Helene made landfall as a Category 4 storm on September 26, 2024, delivering 12-16 inches of rainfall and a 9-foot storm surge to Florida’s Gulf Coast karstic coastlines. During hurricanes, the combined effects of intense rainfall, storm surge, and flooding can enhance groundwater recharge and discharge, intensify aquifer salinization, mobilize contaminants, and deteriorate both groundwater and surface water quality. For example, sudden discharges of nutrient-rich groundwater following extreme precipitation events have been associated with phenomena like planktonic blooms and red tides. Although groundwater-surface water interactions and aquifer salinization in coastal areas are widely studied, most research were conducted during regular weather conditions, potentially underestimating the magnitude of extreme events on coastal aquifer dynamics. Therefore, this study aims to assess both the immediate and long-term effects of hurricanes on hydrogeology and nutrient geochemistry in karstic aquifers. The findings will inform coastal management strategies and improve hydrogeological model predictions, helping to mitigate hurricane-induced impacts on coastal ecosystems and water resources. This project will foster collaboration between two early-career researchers and actively involve undergraduate and graduate students, including those from underrepresented minorities, with results integrated into Texas A&M University at Galveston and Florida Atlantic University courses.

This project will employ interdisciplinary hydrological, geophysical, and geochemical methods to: (1) Evaluate the degree of aquifer salinization and its effects on nutrient speciation, and (2) Quantify groundwater discharge and nutrient fluxes. Electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) will be used to assess aquifer salinization, while radon-222 will be utilized to quantify groundwater discharge. Nutrients and major ion concentrations will be measured from groundwater and surface water samples, with analyses focused on how hydrochemical patterns affect nutrient speciation. The research will be conducted post-hurricane and during baseflow conditions, enabling an assessment of the hydrological disturbances caused by the hurricane on aquifer salinization, groundwater-surface water interactions, and nutrient geochemistry, as well as tracking their progression over time. Additionally, the project will build on previously collected post-storm data from Alabama and Texas, allowing for a comparative analysis of groundwater system responses across different aquifer types (porous and karstic) in the Gulf Coast. This is especially relevant, given that the region is among the most vulnerable in the U.S. to the impacts of extreme weather events and climate change.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The project “Hurricane Impacts on Hydrogeology and Nutrient Geochemistry in Karstic Coastlines” aims to evaluate both the immediate and long-term effects of hurricanes on aquifer salinization, recharge–discharge processes, and nutrient geochemistry in karstic systems. The study focuses on the Wakulla Spring-Apalachee Bay transect in Florida’s Big Bend region, where Hurricane Helene made landfall as a Category 4 storm on September 26, 2024. Geophysical and geochemical investigations were carried out in October 2024, November 2024, January 2025, and May 2025, to assess aquifer recovery over time. Despite advances in understanding aquifer salinization and groundwater-surface water interactions, most existing studies are limited to baseflow conditions or rely on a single disciplinary approach. This project integrates electrical resistivity tomography (ERT), water chemistry (e.g., nitrogen, phosphorus, natrium, chloride), and stable isotope analyses to provide a comprehensive, multidisciplinary perspective on how storm surges and recharge events influence aquifer chemistry and nutrient transformations.

This study was designed to address two specific objectives: (1) to assess the degree of aquifer salinization and its influence on nutrient speciation under post-hurricane and baseflow conditions, and (2) to investigate groundwater discharge behavior during those same periods. The ERT profiles acquired with the ABEM Terrameter LS2 and processed in ZondRes2D revealed clear subsurface resistivity contrasts indicative of variable salinity and lithological conditions along the St. Marks River Park and St. Marks Lighthouse transects. Zones of low resistivity (< 3 Ω·m) correspond to areas of saltwater intrusion within the coastal aquifer, while higher resistivity regions represent fresh to brackish groundwater and unsaturated sediments. Among the different array configurations (Dipole–Dipole and Wenner), the Wenner array provided smoother resistivity gradients, whereas the Dipole–Dipole array enhanced lateral resolution of saline wedge boundaries. Overall, the interpreted sections delineate a landward-thinning saline wedge. Results show a temporary rise in salinity and nitrate concentrations immediately following the hurricane, likely due to oxygenation introduced by storm surge infiltration. In subsequent months, the system reverted to reducing (low oxygen) conditions, leading to denitrification and increased concentrations of ammonia (through mineralization and ion exchange) and phosphate (from dissolution of iron oxides). A low Na/Cl ratio following the storm, which gradually increased over time, further indicates short-term influence of storm surge on groundwater chemistry. Collectively, the data show that nutrient quantity and composition are highly sensitive to redox shifts driven by hurricane-induced oxygenation, which can temporarily alter the N:P ratio in surface waters and increase the risk of algal blooms.

Hydrologic analyses revealed similar recovery patterns. Groundwater levels and fluctuations returned to baseflow within two months of the hurricane. Radon-222 time series measurements in the Wakulla River estuary, used as a tracer for groundwater discharge, closely matched the discharge patterns of nearby Wakulla Spring, indicating that regional hydraulic gradients from the spring primarily control groundwater flow. Complementary data from USGS stations show groundwater levels peaking at 35.89 ft approximately 30 hours after landfall, followed by a gradual decline to baseline conditions within two months. Stable water isotope data further corroborate this rapid recovery, showing isotopically depleted hurricane rainfall mixed with evaporated saline water in October 2024, then a shift toward fresh meteoric recharge by November 2024 and minimal evaporative enrichment by January 2025. By combining discharge and nutrient concentration data, we found that spring-derived nutrient fluxes during the first two months following the hurricane were approximately between 1.5-6 times higher than baseflow depending on the nutrient species, respectively.

Overall, this study demonstrates that the immediate and long-term effects of hurricanes on aquifer salinization and nutrient geochemistry are strongly governed by local geology and storm characteristics. The relatively fast, two-month recovery observed here contrasts with slower responses reported elsewhere and can be attributed to (a) the high hydraulic connectivity and transmissive conduit networks of the karst aquifer, which rapidly flushed residual storm surge, and (b) Hurricane Helene’s short residence time and intense but brief rainfall. In contrast, regions with less transmissive geology or slower-moving hurricanes may experience more prolonged salinization and delayed recovery.
